guppy.e: From a name mistakenly assigned, Girardinus guppii, after biologist Robert J. L. Guppy, to previously assigned Poecilia reticulata.

d.g: a group of Niger-Congo languages spoken primarily in southeastern Mali and northern Ghana
To flow with a bubbling sound.
d.x: The bath water gurgled down the drain.

d.g: To make such a sound.
d.x: The baby gurgled with delight.

d.g: A gurgling sound.

gurgle.e: Back formation from Middle English gurguling (“a rumbling in the belly”). Akin to Middle Dutch gorgelen (“to gurgle”), Middle Low German gorgelen (“to gurgle”), German gurgeln (“to gargle”), and perhaps to Latin gurguliō (“throat”).

d.g: a member of the Nepalese force that has been part of the British army for 200 years;  known for fierceness in combat
Any of various marine fish of the family Triglidae that have a large armored head and fingerlike pectoral fins used for crawling along the sea bottom.
Other fish with appearance like that of members of family Triglidae, such as certain of those in families Dactylopteridae, Peristediidae, and Scorpaenidae.

gurnard.e: From Middle English gurnard, from Old French gournart, from the verb gronir, from Latin grunnīre (“to grunt”). Compare French grondin (“gurnard”), which evolved in a similar way.

d.g: A stretcher having wheeled legs.
d.x: The death row convict was strapped into the gurney in order to be given the lethal injection.

gurney.e: Unknown. Possibly from Gurney cab, a type of horse-drawn cab on wheels named after Theodore Gurney, the US inventor credited with creating and patenting it in about 1883. For the surname, see Gurney.

d.g: In Indian traditions: a spiritual teacher who transmits knowledge to a shishya.
d.x: Many of the deities and beliefs recorded by the guru are in fact unknown to the common people, and some represent the esoteric knowledge of only a few guru.

d.g: Any general teacher (as a term of respect).
An influential advisor or mentor.
d.x: Many oenophiles rely on the ratings and recommendations of wine guru Robert Parker when selecting the perfect bottle.

d.g: A fraudster or conman relying on a projected air of confidence in an obscure field.

guru.e: Borrowed from Hindi गुरु (guru) / Punjabi ਗੁਰੂ (gurū), from Sanskrit गुरु (guru, “venerable, respectable”), originally "heavy" and in this sense cognate to English grieve and, more distantly, brute. Doublet of grave. …

d.g: A sudden rapid outflow.
To flow forth suddenly, in great volume.
d.x: Water gushed out of the broken pipe.

d.g: To send (something) flowing forth suddenly in great volume.
d.x: A beautiful spring gushed water from the ground in this mountainous sector of Polk County, inspiring the name of the place.

d.g: To ejaculate during orgasm.
d.x: Her orgasm exploded over her, making her writhe and cry out his name. She gushed over his hand, her cunt gripping and releasing his invading fingers.

gush.e: From Middle English guschen, gusshen, gosshien, perhaps from Middle Dutch guysen (“to flow out with a gurgling sound, gush”) or Old Norse gusa (“to gush”), ultimately imitative. Compare Old Norse geysa (“to gush”), German gießen (“to pour”), Old English ġēotan ("to pour"; > English yote). Related to gust.

d.g: One who gushes (makes an excessive display of enthusiasm, praise, or sentiment).
An oil well that has a natural flow and so requires no pumping.
A small piece of cloth inserted in a garment, for the purpose of strengthening some part or giving it a tapering enlargement cf. godet.
A gousset, a piece of mail providing protection where armor plates meet.
A kind of bracket, or angular part, fastened in the angles of a structure to give strength or stiffness; especially, the part joining the barrel and the fire box of a locomotive boiler.
An ordinary on a coat of arms, resembling a gusset (see usage notes).

gusset.e: From Middle English gusset, gysset, from Old French gosset, gousset (“the hollow of the armpit”), diminutive of gose, gosse (“bean pod, hull, husk”).

d.g: A strong, abrupt rush of wind.
Any rush or outburst (of water, emotion, etc.).
d.x: they are merely driven about by every sudden gust and impulse of the mind

d.g: To blow in gusts.
d.x: Do the dryers disperse bacteria and viruses through the restroom, like autumn breezes gusting leaves across a lawn?

d.g: Relish, enjoyment, appreciation.
d.x:
, "The Spirit of Grace"
An ox will relish the tender flesh of kids with as much gust and appetite.

gust.e: Apparently from an unrecorded Middle English *gust, from Old Norse gustr (“a gust, blast”), from Proto-Germanic *gustiz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰew-. Cognate with Icelandic gustur (“gust of wind”). …

d.g: The act of tasting.
d.x: The organ of gustation is not, therefore, restricted to the production of that sense, but participates in the sense of touch.

d.g: The ability to taste flavors; the sense of taste.

gustation.e: Proto-Indo-European *ǵews-der. Latin gustō Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *-Hō Proto-Indo-European *-tiHō Proto-Italic *-tiō Latin -tiō Latin gustatio, gustationisbor. English gustation Borrowed from Latin gustatio, gustationis.

d.g: the last king of Sweden to have any real political power (1882-1973)
Enthusiasm; enjoyment, vigor.
d.x: He sang with more gusto than talent.

d.g: An individual's fondness or liking of a particular flavour
d.x: Why should you force wine upon us? We are not all of your gusto.

d.g: The style in which a work is done, artistic style. (occasionally) the prevailing style in matters of taste.
d.x: The Designs..are of very mean Gusto.

gusto.e: Borrowed from Italian gusto, from Latin gustus (“taste”). Doublet of cost (see Etymology 3 there).

d.g: The alimentary canal, especially the intestine.
The abdomen of a person, especially one that is enlarged.
d.x: You've developed quite a beer gut since I last met you.

d.g: The intestines of an animal used to make strings of a tennis racket or violin, etc.
A person's emotional, visceral self.
d.x: I have a funny feeling in my gut.

gut.e: From Middle English gut, gutte, gotte, from Old English gutt (usually in plural guttas (“guts, entrails”)), from Proto-Germanic *gut-, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰewd- (“to pour”). Related to English gote (“drain”), Old English ġēotan (“to pour”). More at gote, yote. …

d.g: German printer who was the first in Europe to print using movable type and the first to use a press (1400-1468)
United States folk singer and songwriter (1912-1967)
sticky perennial herbs and subshrubs of western North America and warm South America
The state or condition of being gutless; cowardice.
plural of gut
The entrails or contents of the abdomen.
Courage; determination.
d.x: It must have taken some guts to speak in front of that audience.

d.g: Content, substance.
d.x: His speech had no guts in it.

d.g: The state or condition of being gutsy.

gutsiness.e: English gutsy Proto-Germanic *-inōną Proto-Indo-European *-dyé- Proto-Germanic *-atjaną Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Germanic *-þuz Proto-Germanic *-assuz Proto-Germanic *-inassuz Proto-West Germanic *-nassī Old English -nes Middle English -nesse English -ness English gutsiness From gutsy + -ness.

d.g: A prepared channel in a surface, especially at the side of a road adjacent to a curb, intended for the drainage of water.
d.x: They a not so clean as they might be, since the water [is] carried off by only one gutter, in the centre of t[he] street

d.g: A ditch along the side of a road.
d.x: In nearly all of the towns the gutters are filled with vegetation, or have been neglected for so long a time that the roadway becomes its own drainage bed.

d.g: A duct or channel beneath the eaves of a building to carry rain water; eavestrough.
d.x: The gutters must be cleared of leaves a few times a year.

d.g: A groove down the sides of a bowling lane.
d.x: You can decide to use the bumpers to avoid the ball going down the gutter every time.

gutter.e: From Middle English gutter, guttur, goter, from Anglo-Norman guttere, from Old French goutiere (French gouttière), ultimately from Latin gutta (“drop”).

d.g: A person of the lowest social or economic class.
d.x: Do not worry, Mrs Kane, we will return you a different boy. The guttersnipe you bring us will not be the boy you get back.

d.g: widely distributed family of chiefly tropical trees and shrubs and vines that produce oils and resins and some usable timber
used in some classifications;  coextensive with Parietales
Alternative spelling of guv'nor.
An effigy of a man burned on a bonfire on the anniversary of the Gunpowder Plot (5th November).
A person of eccentric appearance or dress; a "fright".
d.x:
“But shan’t I look a guy?”
“Not a bit of it. Jist the very kick!”

d.g: A man or boy; a fellow.
d.x: “You don't say so? I thought he was some guy from Pennsylvania.”

d.g: A person (see usage notes).
d.x: You know, I don't believe any girl ever had any better friends than you two guys

guy.e: Coined by semantic widening from the name of Guy Fawkes (1570–1606), an English Catholic executed for his role in the Gunpowder Plot, which also came to refer to effigies of his image burned annually on Guy Fawkes Night. …

d.g: a republic in northeastern South America;  formerly part of the British Empire, but it achieved independence from the United Kingdom in 1966
A flat-topped seamount.

guyot.e: Coined by Harry Hammond Hess circa 1965 due to their similar appearance to Guyot Hall, the flat-topped geology building at Princeton University, which was in turn named after Swiss-American geologist Arnold Henry Guyot.

d.g: Somebody or something which guzzles.
A device placed in arid regions to catch water for wildlife to drink from.
d.x: Quail require little water, so there is no point to putting in a guzzler if there is any permanent water within travel range.

guzzler.e: English guzzle Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzijos Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English guzzler From guzzle + -er.

d.g: present participle and gerund of guzzle
greedy eating or drinking
d.x: […] there ain't a housekeeper, no nor a lodger in our street, don't know that I lost money by that man, and by his guzzlings […]

d.g: To make a sound as of liquid being poured from a small-necked container
To pour from a container and make this sound
The sound of liquid being poured.
eat greedily

guttle.e: The verb is possibly derived from gut (“belly”) + -le (frequentative suffix), perhaps influenced by guzzle (“to drink or eat quickly, voraciously, or to excess; to gulp down; to swallow greedily, continually, or with gusto”). The noun is derived from the verb.

d.g: To drink or eat quickly, voraciously, or to excess; to gulp down; to swallow greedily, continually, or with gusto.
d.x: No more her care shall fill the hollow tray, / To fat the guzzling hogs with floods of whey.

d.g: To consume alcoholic beverages, especially frequently or habitually.
d.x: A comparison more properly bestowed on those that came to guzzle in his wine cellar.

d.g: To consume anything quickly, greedily, or to excess, as if with insatiable thirst; often said of gas-powered vehicles.
d.x: This car just guzzles petrol.

d.g: To flow copiously; to spray out.
d.x: Blood guzzled from the wound.

guzzle.e: Probably imitative of the sound of drinking eagerly; or from Old French gouziller, gosillier (“to pass through the throat”), from gosier (“throat”), and akin to Italian gozzo (“throat; a bird's crop”). First attested in 1576.
